title: Hair relaxer made Black women beautiful, and made them pay with their health
dek: Chemical hair relaxers built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and have also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is at once an economic ladder and a bodily cost.
why: This episode has medium information density, but it tells the story of how a single product can be empowerment and harm at the same time in very concrete terms — suited to listeners interested in consumer history, public health and the racial economy.
who: Listeners interested in the intersection of consumer history, public health and the racial economy; people working in beauty, personal care or health consumer goods can also see the interaction between regulation and markets.
skip: The roughly two-minute production credits at the end can be skipped.

points.body: Chemical hair relaxers have a nickname in the salon: creamy crack, because they are said to be as addictive as cocaine — once you start, it's hard to stop. When you do stop, the new growth meets the already-straightened dead hair and breaks at the line of demarcation. For a week before use you can't wash your hair or scratch your scalp, or you'll get burned; when it's applied you have to avoid the scalp and coat only the hair shaft, but leave it too long near the ends and it still stings. In the episode the host recalls being slathered with relaxer for the first time at age 9, having already seen women in the salon cry out in pain.

points.h: From African hair tradition to a survival strategy
points.body: Hair historian Lorie Tharps says starting the story with slavery is starting at chapter two and missing chapter one: Africa already had rich hair traditions, and hair connected tribe, family and identity. After being enslaved in America, straightening went from self-expression to survival strategy — because they were told their hair was inferior, ugly, more like an animal's, and straightening became a visual way of proving "we are equal to you." They used butter instead of palm oil, made shampoo from cornmeal and kerosene, used butter knives as crude curling irons, and wrapped hair around thread to straighten it.

The methods these enslaved people invented were good enough to make them the barbers and wig makers of choice for white clients. White people paid for their craft, and that channel let many of them buy their own freedom. Tharps says some early Black colleges and institutions were funded or founded by Black barbers, such as Wilberforce University — an HBCU wholly owned and operated by African Americans, built in large part on barbering income. But the irony is that these Black barbers did not cut Black hair at the time; they served white clients.

points.h: The hot comb gives way to an accidental discovery
points.body: Madame CJ Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone used the hot comb plus hair oil to produce sleek straight hair, turning scattered straightening methods into a system, and Walker became the first self-made millionaire woman in America, of any race. But the hot comb's effect was temporary — sweat, humidity or rain restored the original state. In the early 1900s, Cleveland tailor Garrett Augustus Morgan wanted to invent a substance that kept high-speed machines and needles from damaging wool and other animal fur, and after trying a formula he found the fur had straightened. He tested it first on a neighbour's dog, then on his own hair, and both straightened — he had accidentally discovered that lye (sodium hydroxide) plus other ingredients could straighten hair.

points.h: The man who put relaxer on drugstore shelves
points.body: George Johnson is called by Tharps the Madam CJ Walker of his era. A barber doing homemade conks came to this chemist and asked whether he could make something fast and easy, and that produced Ultra Wave for men, followed by Ultra Sheen for women. Unlike the temporary hot comb and dangerous homemade lye formulas, Ultra Sheen was long-lasting, safer, and available in any drugstore — no salon needed. That privacy mattered: straightening hair with chemicals carried shame, and doing it at home meant no one saw you going to the salon.

points.h: Profits flowed back to the Black community, then regulators took notice
points.body: Johnson put profits back into the Black community: Soul Train, Essence Magazine, Chicago's Independence Bank — then the largest Black-owned bank in the country, lending to homeowners and entrepreneurs redlined by white banks; funding Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesse Jackson; employing hundreds of Black and brown workers who couldn't find jobs because of racial discrimination, giving them profit sharing, full health insurance, on-site nurses, full college tuition, paid maternity and sick leave, and four-day weekends every holiday. In 1964 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange. But in 1975 the FTC required Johnson to put a warning label on the outside of relaxer packaging saying the product contained lye and could be harmful — while Revlon's relaxer, which also contained lye, was not immediately required to add a label, a delay of nearly two years.

points.h: The civil rights movement flipped the politics of straight hair
points.body: During the Black Power era, Black people decided straightening had solved nothing — from Madam CJ Walker's hot comb to relaxers, every method had been tried and it still hadn't worked. So came a simpler and more radical idea: I will no longer straighten my hair, I will use my hair as protest. Black hair grows up and out; it doesn't make you smaller, it makes you taller. The political flip was so complete that some Black people with naturally straight hair got perms, because not everyone's hair can grow into an Angela Davis-style afro. But the beauty industry then commodified the afro, selling wigs and marketing it as beauty and empowerment while also pulling its teeth and turning it into just another fashion trend. By the 1980s, straight hair was back.

points.h: A 34,000-woman study: risk up two and a half times
points.body: A large 2022 study followed 34,000 women and found that frequent users of chemical hair straightening products — most of them Black women — were two and a half times as likely to develop uterine cancer as never-users. New York Times Magazine contributor Linda Varosa says this was the first high-quality study to link straightening products, Black women and two cancers (endometrial and uterine). The research also linked these products to fibroids, which Black women develop at far higher rates than other women. The study shows correlation, not causation, but Tharps thinks agonising over correlation versus causation misses the point: she thinks the red flag should simply be waved, with warnings on packaging, on labels and in salons.
